title: Highland Foundry Ltd. (Aug 1994 TCC) Tax Court Ruling
subject: Metal foundry SR&ED appeal examining whether casting process improvements and alloy testing qualified as SR&ED.
outcome: Appeal allowed in part; court found specific systematic foundry experiments qualified while routine production did not.
summary: The Highland Foundry Ltd. decision of the Tax Court of Canada (August 1994) guides Canadian corporations claiming SR&ED investment tax credits on prototype capital expenditures. The Court held that the "all or substantially all" test is applied when the money is spent, not over the asset's useful life, so a genuine prototype stays eligible despite continued commercial use.
metaDescription: Analyze the August 1994 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for Highland Foundry Ltd. on Canadian R&D tax credit eligibility.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The judgment of the Tax Court of Canada in Highland Foundry Ltd. v. Her Majesty The Queen (Court File No. 92-264, judgment rendered by McArthur J.T.C.C. on August 15, 1994, concerning the 1985, 1986, and 1987 taxation years) represents a foundational precedent within Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence on the timing of the "all or substantially all" test for capital expenditures. Based in Surrey, British Columbia, Highland Foundry Ltd. was a family-operated foundry business that produced metal castings by pouring molten metal into cold moulds made from "green sand" imported from the United States at approximately $113 per ton; for the most part, its castings were used in the pulp and paper industry. Because contact with the molten metal contaminated the sand and left it of limited further use, the appellant, with the assistance of an employee engineer, undertook research and experimentation to develop a system to reclaim the contaminated sand for reuse; for its 1985, 1986, and 1987 taxation years, it claimed Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) in respect of capital expenditures of $10,851 (laboratory equipment used during the research phase to monitor whether the sand was contaminated), $104,084 and $90,148 (construction of the prototype sand refiner), a claim first made in 1989 following a change in the appellant's accountants.

The Minister of National Revenue (then administering the Income Tax Act through Revenue Canada, now the Canada Revenue Agency or CRA) reassessed the appellant for the 1985, 1986, and 1987 taxation years, disallowing the capital costs claimed for ITC purposes; the Minister later withdrew its disallowance of a separate $26,888 current expense claimed in 1987. The scientific eligibility of the work was not in dispute: the Crown acknowledged that the research to develop the refiner was valid SR&ED, did not dispute that the capital expenses were used in the research and development of the refiner, and did not dispute the facts set out in the appellant's written argument. Central to Revenue Canada's assessment position was its reliance on the departmental interpretation in Interpretation Bulletin IT-151R3 that the "all or substantially all" test for capital property looks to the intended use of the asset over its expected useful life (normally at least 90 per cent of the time for SR&ED); because the refiner and laboratory equipment remained in regular foundry use after the research was completed, the Minister argued that the expenditures were not all or substantially all attributable to SR&ED, that the refiner was never a prototype, and that the assets should receive the graduated capital cost allowance rather than the accelerated SR&ED write-off.

During the 1985, 1986, and 1987 taxation years at issue in Highland Foundry Ltd., the governing statutory framework in Canada comprised section 37 (the Court identified as relevant paragraph 37(1)(b), governing expenditures of a capital nature, and clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A), which limits SR&ED expenditures to those incurred for and all or substantially all attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED, or to the provision of premises, facilities or equipment for that prosecution) and section 127 (governing Investment Tax Credits) of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, as amended, and subsequently R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), read in conjunction with section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Under Regulation 2900(1), eligible "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. This statutory definition encompasses three core branches of eligible inquiry: basic research, defined under paragraph 2900(1)(a) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research, defined under paragraph 2900(1)(b) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and development, defined under paragraph 2900(1)(c), in the version quoted by the Court, as use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes.

Crucially, Regulation 2900(1), as quoted in the judgment, expressly includes activities with respect to engineering or design, operations research, mathematical analysis or computer programming and psychological research where such activities are undertaken directly in support of basic research, applied research, or development. Conversely, paragraphs 2900(1)(d) through (j) exclude market research or sales promotion, research in the social sciences or humanities, prospecting, style changes, and routine data collection, together with the two exclusions quoted by the Court: quality control or routine testing of materials, devices or products (paragraph (e)), and the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (paragraph (h)). While subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act subsequently consolidated the text of Regulation 2900(1) directly into the statute, the substantive eligibility test—later articulated by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998) as requiring scientific or technological uncertainty, a systematic investigation by experiment or analysis, and work undertaken to achieve a scientific or technological advancement—was not at issue in Highland Foundry Ltd., because the Crown conceded that the refiner research was valid SR&ED.

The final holding of the Tax Court of Canada in Highland Foundry Ltd. established two related legal propositions concerning capital expenditures on SR&ED. First, regarding the time frame for the "all or substantially all" test in clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A), the Court held that the determination must be made at the time the money is expended—over the period during which the prosecution of SR&ED or the construction is taking place—and not over the full useful life of the asset or years later with the benefit of hindsight; finding the statute unclear on this point, the Court resolved the ambiguity in favour of the taxpayer, relying on Johns-Manville Canada Inc. v. The Queen ([1985] 2 S.C.R. 46), and the decision did not rely on or refer to Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue (88 DTC 1363), which concerns the taxpayer's evidentiary burden on scientific eligibility—an issue that did not arise in Highland Foundry Ltd. because the Crown conceded eligibility. Applying that test, the Court found that, at the time the expenditures were incurred for the prototype refiner and the laboratory equipment, they were made for the prosecution of SR&ED and would not have been incurred but for the SR&ED, so that they were incurred "all or substantially all" for SR&ED and the appeals were allowed with costs (the conclusion at paragraph [37] states the amounts as $11,688, $111,148 and $95,151, which differ from the $10,851, $104,084 and $90,148 set out at paragraph [1]).

Second, and most significantly for the treatment of prototypes, at paragraphs [18] to [20] of the Highland Foundry judgment, the Tax Court addressed whether the sand refiner was a "prototype" notwithstanding its continued use in the foundry business; the judgment does not discuss testimony by Revenue Canada (now CRA) employees tendered by the Crown as expert witnesses. The Court observed that rules of statutory interpretation require words to be read in their ordinary and grammatical sense unless the context or object of the statute suggests otherwise, and that this rule is also cogent when interpreting Interpretation Bulletins and Information Circulars, which, while not law, can be very useful in interpreting the legislation. Applying the Concise Oxford Dictionary definition of a prototype—an original thing in relation to a copy or improved form; a trial model or preliminary version—the Court held that the refiner easily fell within the meaning of "prototype", regardless of the fact that the appellant continued to use it in its business. In Highland Foundry, the Court described the refiner as the original form of the process and a patented trial model that had provided a test of the feasibility of the concept, and agreed with the appellant that an asset having value beyond its experimental stage is not, for that reason, disentitled to SR&ED treatment at that point in time. The prototype analysis at paragraphs [18] to [20] of Highland Foundry does not concern expert evidence, and nothing in the decision supports describing it as the doctrinal foundation for later Tax Court of Canada rulings on the evidence of CRA employees—such as Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC, Docket 2011-2054(IT)G) and HLP Solutions Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC, Docket 2012-671(IT)G)—which addressed the Crown's reliance on its own employees as ostensibly independent experts.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A granular examination of the dispute in Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994), in which the taxpayer succeeded and the only contested issue was the timing of the "all or substantially all" test, does not itself reveal taxpayer deficiencies; the six interconnected legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies discussed below are drawn from broader SR&ED practice and routinely trigger audit denials by the CRA and adverse holdings in the Tax Court of Canada. Understanding the mechanics, origins, and downstream implications of these failures is essential for structuring defensible SR&ED claims within heavy manufacturing, metallurgy, and custom industrial fabrication environments.
Failure to Distinguish Technological Uncertainty from Routine Metallurgical Engineering and Shop-Floor Troubleshooting

In specialty foundry operations involving iron, steel, and nickel-based alloys, technical complexity is inherent to daily production. However, under Regulation 2900(1)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations (and now subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act), high technical difficulty or elevated defect rates in commercial casting do not equate to "technological uncertainty". A genuine technological uncertainty exists only where the probability of achieving a given technical objective or design specification cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or standard engineering practice within the relevant industry.

A primary deficiency in industrial foundry claims arises when taxpayers conflate routine process optimization with experimental development. When a foundry accepts a commercial order for a complex valve body, sawmill component, or marine propeller casting using an established ASTM-grade alloy (such as CF8M stainless steel or Monel 400), encountering shrinkage porosity, hot tearing, sand inclusions, or dimensional warping during the initial pour is a standard production problem. Modifying the gating system, resizing risers, adding chills, or adjusting pouring temperatures within established metallurgical parameters constitutes routine engineering or quality control and routine testing excluded under Regulation 2900(1)(e). Disqualification occurs because the taxpayer's technical narratives describe product defects and physical corrective actions without establishing why the underlying metallurgical or thermodynamic system behaviour was unpredictable under existing phase diagrams, solidification models, or published foundry data.
Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation and Systematic Investigation

In alignment with the Tax Court of Canada's jurisprudence in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. (1988) and Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994)—although the latter did not consider this requirement, because the Crown conceded that the refiner research was valid SR&ED—the statutory phrase "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" requires a disciplined, scientific methodology. In shop-floor manufacturing disputes, claims fail when the taxpayer's development process resembles ad hoc trial-and-error rather than structured experimentation.

Specifically, when a foundry pours a casting, observes a defect via non-destructive testing (such as radiography or ultrasonic inspection), and alters three or four process variables simultaneously—such as changing the sand binder ratio, pouring temperature, and ladle inoculation all at once—simply to get a passing component shipped before a customer deadline, the activity lacks analytical rigour. Without isolating independent variables, formulating an explicit technical hypothesis prior to each trial heat, predicting the microstructural or mechanical mechanism, and conducting quantitative post-test analysis (such as metallographic microscopy, Charpy V-notch impact testing, or chemical spectroscopy) to correlate the variable change to the observed phenomenon, the taxpayer cannot prove to the Court that a systematic investigation occurred.
Conflation of Experimental Prototypes with Custom Commercial Production Runs

One of the sharpest points of legal and technical friction in Highland Foundry Ltd.—explicitly addressed at paragraphs [18] to [20] of the ruling—concerned the legal and technical characterization of "prototypes". In a custom jobbing foundry, the taxpayer rarely manufactures thousands of identical consumer units; rather, it produces small batches or single custom castings tailored to severe-service engineering requirements. This operational reality creates a dual-sided legal trap involving both administrative overreach by the tax authority and over-claiming by the taxpayer.

On the administrative side, during the audit and objection stages of Highland Foundry, Revenue Canada relied on the useful-life interpretation of the "all or substantially all" test set out at paragraphs 21 to 23 of Interpretation Bulletin IT-151R3, whereas Information Circular IC 86-4R2 (dated August 29, 1988), also placed before the Court, described prototypes as providing a test of the feasibility of a concept or hypothesis within experimental development. Under IT-151R3, a capital asset normally had to be used at least 90 per cent of the time throughout its expected useful life for SR&ED, and expenditures on projects reasonably expected to result in property used in the taxpayer's business or sold were viewed as not all or substantially all attributable to SR&ED, unless the SR&ED portion could be segregated as described in IC 86-4R2. Consequently, because the prototype refiner and the laboratory equipment continued in day-to-day use in the foundry after the research was completed, the Minister disallowed the capital costs and argued that the refiner was never a prototype. At paragraphs [18] to [20], the Tax Court exposed the legal flaw in this administrative posture: applying the ordinary dictionary meaning of "prototype" (a trial model or preliminary version), the Court held that the refiner easily fell within that meaning regardless of its continued use in the business, and that an asset having value beyond its experimental stage is not thereby disentitled to SR&ED treatment; the judgment refers to no expert witness testimony.

Conversely, on the taxpayer compliance side, although the Court did not decide this point, the commercial production exclusion in paragraph 2900(1)(h) means a taxpayer may still fail on the merits where it claims entire commercial production runs or multi-unit customer orders as prototype development. Once the first experimental casting or trial heat resolves the technological uncertainty and validates the metallurgical process parameters, every subsequent casting poured using that validated protocol represents excluded commercial production under Regulation 2900(1)(h), regardless of whether the customer refers to the initial batch as a pre-production or prototype order.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Retrospective Reconstruction

In Tax Court appeals involving historical taxation years—such as the 1985, 1986, and 1987 taxation years decided in August 1994 in Highland Foundry Ltd.—the passage of seven to nine years between the shop-floor activity and the judgment can severely test the reliability of oral testimony, although in Highland Foundry Ltd. itself the respondent did not dispute the facts set out in the appellant's written argument. Where a taxpayer relies on retrospective project summaries drafted years after the fact by external tax consultants or senior managers without dated, contemporaneous technical records generated during the actual experimental work, the Court assigns minimal evidentiary weight to self-serving oral recollections.

In a foundry setting, this evidentiary deficiency manifests when the only surviving documents are standard commercial shop travelers, customer invoices, shipping manifests, and pass/fail quality assurance certificates. While standard shop travelers prove that a casting was poured on a certain date, they do not document the technological uncertainty, the hypothesis being tested, the experimental parameters deviated from standard practice, or the analytical conclusions drawn from failed heats. Without dated engineering notebooks, metallurgical failure analysis reports, or experimental heat logs created contemporaneously with the work in 1985, 1986, and 1987, a taxpayer in a comparable dispute may fail to discharge its prima facie burden of demolishing the Minister's assumptions of fact—an issue that did not arise in Highland Foundry Ltd., where the facts were not in dispute.
Inadequate Financial Cost Segregation and Expenditure Attribution

As underscored by Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, establishing scientific eligibility is only half of the statutory requirement; the taxpayer must independently prove expenditure eligibility under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. In Highland Foundry Ltd., expenditure eligibility was the sole contested issue: the Minister argued that capital equipment that continued in commercial use for many years could not be all or substantially all attributable to SR&ED, and the Court rejected that argument by measuring the test at the time the expenditures were incurred.

Under the statutory rules governing the 1985 to 1987 period—prior to the introduction of the simplified proxy method in December 1992, when all claimants were required to use the traditional overhead allocation method—expenditures qualified only to the extent they were incurred "all or substantially all" (interpreted by Revenue Canada in IT-151R3 as 90% or more) for, and attributable to, the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada or the provision of premises, facilities or equipment for that prosecution under clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A); in Highland Foundry Ltd., the Court noted, citing Wood v. M.N.R. (1987), that "substantially all" does not lend itself to a simple mathematical formula. Disqualification occurs when taxpayers utilize arbitrary percentage estimates, such as claiming a flat percentage of the foundry manager's, metallurgist's, and furnace operators' annual salaries alongside a generalized allocation of furnace electricity and moulding sand, without contemporaneous time-tracking sheets or job-costing ledgers tied to specific eligible experimental projects. Furthermore, claiming the cost of raw alloy ingots and moulding materials that are ultimately incorporated into castings sold commercially without accounting for the value of the salable commercial output violates statutory expenditure eligibility rules.
Contractual Ambiguity and Funded Research or Contract Payment Exclusions

In the custom foundry and heavy manufacturing sector, technical development is frequently initiated in response to a customer's purchase order for components operating in extreme environments, such as high-pressure safety valves or corrosive pulp digester fittings. Under subsection 127(18) and subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by any "contract payment" (defined in subsection 127(9))—broadly, an amount paid or payable to the taxpayer for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of the payer—as well as any government or non-government assistance.

When a manufacturer's commercial contracts or purchase orders are imprecisely drafted—stating, for instance, that the customer is paying a tooling, engineering, and prototype development fee or acquiring ownership of all custom patterns, metallurgical specifications, and test data—the tax authority routinely characterizes the transaction as contract SR&ED performed on behalf of the customer. Consequently, the customer's payments are treated as contract payments that reduce the manufacturer's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar, eliminating the ITC claim even if the underlying metallurgical work satisfies the scientific criteria of Regulation 2900(1).
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each core legal and procedural requirement implicated in Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994) and broader SR&ED practice against the typical taxpayer or tax authority failure and the corresponding judicial standard of proof applied by the Tax Court of Canada (only the prototype and expenditure-eligibility rows reflect issues actually decided in Highland Foundry Ltd.).

Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof

cells: Technological Uncertainty
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1)(c); Income Tax Act s. 248(1)
Conflating high casting scrap rates, complex part geometry, or routine gating/risering adjustments with genuine technological uncertainty.

The taxpayer must prove through objective baseline evidence that standard metallurgical/engineering knowledge and published industry standards were insufficient to predict how to achieve the specified technical objectives.
Systematic Investigation by Experiment or Analysis
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1); Sass Manufacturing Ltd. (88 DTC 1363)
Relying on ad hoc shop-floor trial-and-error, altering multiple foundry variables simultaneously without a documented hypothesis or analytical isolation of variables.

Credible evidence must demonstrate a structured scientific protocol: observation of problem, formulation of a clear hypothesis, controlled experimental testing, and rigorous quantitative analysis of results.
Technological Advancement
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1)(c); Income Tax Act s. 248(1)
Claiming commercial product qualification or standard ASTM alloy compliance rather than an advancement in underlying metallurgical or process technology.

Evidence must establish that the investigation generated new technological knowledge advancing the taxpayer's understanding of material science or process engineering beyond standard industry practice, even if the project failed commercially.
Eligibility of Prototypes vs. Commercial Production
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1)(h); Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994), paras. [18]–[20]

Crown Failure: Applying the IT-151R3 useful-life reading of the "all or substantially all" test to deny the capital cost of a prototype because it remained in commercial use, and arguing it was never a prototype. Taxpayer Failure: Failing to cut off SR&ED claims once experimental validation ends and commercial production begins.

Prototypes must be evaluated under the ordinary and grammatical (dictionary) meaning of the term rather than the Minister's IT-151R3 useful-life interpretation; continued commercial use does not disqualify a prototype, and "all or substantially all" is determined when the expenditure is incurred; however, the taxpayer must strictly segregate experimental validation heats from commercial order fulfillment.
Contemporaneous Technical Documentation
Income Tax Act s. 37(1), s. 230(1); Tax Court Evidentiary Rules
Relying on retrospective narratives prepared years after the 1985–1987 tax years and generic commercial shop travelers lacking experimental hypotheses or test data.

While not an absolute statutory prerequisite in 1985–1987, contemporaneous, dated experimental records (heat logs, lab microscopy, failure analyses) are practically essential to corroborate oral testimony and demolish the Minister's assumptions.
Expenditure Eligibility & Cost Segregation
Income Tax Act s. 37(1), s. 127(9); Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(2)–(3)
Using arbitrary year-end percentage estimates for shop wages, furnace utilities, and raw materials without segregating commercial foundry jobs from SR&ED trials.
The taxpayer must provide verifiable cost-accounting records (project timecards, segregated work orders, material consumption logs) proving direct attribution to eligible SR&ED activities.
Impartiality of Expert Witnesses
Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994), paras. [18]–[20] (prototype meaning only; no expert evidence was addressed); HLP Solutions Inc. (2015 TCC)

Crown Failure: Tendering internal Revenue Canada / CRA employees as expert witnesses whose technical opinions are constrained by departmental administrative policy rather than independent scientific judgment.

An expert witness testifying in the Tax Court of Canada owes an overriding duty of impartiality to the Court and must base opinions strictly on scientific "first principles" and ordinary statutory meaning, setting aside CRA policy guidelines (a duty drawn from later jurisprudence such as HLP Solutions; Highland Foundry Ltd. supports only the related points that Interpretation Bulletins and Information Circulars are not law and that statutory words carry their ordinary meaning).

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994) into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian corporate taxpayers, the following two applied case studies examine high-risk industrial scenarios that illustrate legal, technical, and evidentiary vulnerabilities commonly scrutinized by the CRA and the Tax Court of Canada, most of which were not at issue in Highland Foundry Ltd. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, technical documentation, commercial contracting, and expenditure tracking.
Case Study 1: Specialty Metallurgical Foundry — Experimental Development of Super-Duplex Stainless Steel Valve Castings for Subsea Sour Service
Baseline Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Pacific Alloy Castings Inc. ("Pacific Alloy"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) operating a specialty sand-casting and investment-casting foundry in British Columbia, receives a $480,000 purchase order from a petrochemical valve manufacturer ("ValveCo") to supply twelve thick-walled (150 mm section thickness) pilot-operated safety relief valve bodies. The customer requires the castings to meet a modified hyper-duplex stainless steel specification capable of withstanding extreme hydrogen sulfide (H2S) sour service at −46°C while maintaining a 50/50 austenite-ferrite phase balance and zero intermetallic sigma (σ) or chi (χ) phase precipitation at the thermal center of the 150 mm cross-section.

In its initial unguided execution, Pacific Alloy handles the project through its standard commercial production workflow and commits four fatal compliance errors. First, regarding governance and execution, the foundry metallurgist assigns a regular commercial job number (JOB-8841) to the entire 12-unit order. Over six months, the shop pours 19 heats across 28 castings to yield 12 acceptable units, as the first 16 castings fail destructive Charpy impact testing and metallographic etching due to severe sigma-phase embrittlement and nitrogen gas porosity in the heavy wall sections. Second, regarding documentation, the metallurgist adjusts chromium-molybdenum-tungsten-nitrogen (Cr-Mo-W-N) charge chemistries, ladle argon-oxygen decarburization (AOD) practices, mould thermal conductivity (switching from silica to chromite and zircon sand blends), and water-quench agitation parameters directly on the shop floor, yet the only records kept are standard commercial heat sheets and pass/fail test certificates. Third, regarding contractual terms, ValveCo's purchase order states that Pacific Alloy will design gating, perform prototype qualification testing, and deliver 12 certified castings for $40,000 per unit, with all casting procedures and test data becoming the property of ValveCo. Fourth, at year-end, Pacific Alloy claims the entire $610,000 cost of all 19 heats (comprising labour, alloys, furnace power, sand, and non-destructive testing) on Form T661 as an eligible SR&ED prototype project, without reducing the claim for the $480,000 received from ValveCo.

Under the Highland Foundry decision and general SR&ED principles, the CRA would likely disallow most or all of this claim during a combined technical and financial review, although Highland Foundry Ltd. itself confirms that later commercial use does not, by itself, defeat SR&ED treatment of expenditures incurred while the prosecution of SR&ED was ongoing. The lack of isolated hypotheses makes the 19 heats appear as routine trial-and-error troubleshooting; claiming all 28 castings (including the 12 commercially delivered units) violates the commercial production exclusion of subsection 248(1) (formerly Regulation 2900(1)(h)); the lack of segregated accounting invalidates the labour and material pool; and ValveCo's purchase order terms trigger the contract payment reduction under subsection 127(18).
Step 1: Project Governance and Gate-Review Architecture

To establish a legally defensible boundary between eligible experimental development and excluded commercial production, Pacific Alloy must implement a formal Two-Track Stage-Gate Governance Protocol before melting a single kilogram of metal. At Gate 0 (Baseline Literature and System Uncertainty Audit), prior to project initiation, the Chief Metallurgist conducts and archives a formal literature search of ASM Handbooks, ASTM A890/A995 standards, and thermodynamic phase-diagram software (such as Thermo-Calc). The audit documents that existing metallurgical models cannot predict the kinetics of sigma-phase nucleation in hyper-duplex alloys with > 0.40 wt% N when solidification cooling rates fall below 0.15°C/s in 150 mm sand-cast cross-sections. This establishes the technological baseline and isolates the technological uncertainty—specifically, the system-level conflict between high nitrogen solubility required to stabilize austenite and slow thermal dissipation in thick sand moulds driving brittle intermetallic precipitation.

At Gate 1 (Segregation of SR&ED Project from Commercial Order), management splits the workflow into two distinct internal charters: an SR&ED Project Charter (SRED-2026-04), authorized exclusively to investigate the thermodynamic and metallurgical kinetics of thick-section hyper-duplex solidification using sacrificial stepped test blocks and instrumented experimental castings; and a Commercial Production Order (PROD-8841), which is placed on hold until SRED-2026-04 achieves technological advancement and freezes the validated Standard Operating Procedure (SOP). Finally, at Gate 2 (Experimental Cut-Off and Commercial Transition), as soon as an experimental casting trial validates the hypothesis and satisfies the target microstructure (50/50 ± 5% ferrite-austenite, < 0.5% intermetallic phase, and > 65 J impact toughness at −46°C), the Chief Metallurgist signs a formal SR&ED Technical Freeze Certificate. Every heat poured after that timestamp is charged strictly to PROD-8841 and excluded from the SR&ED claim.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Evidence Protocols

To satisfy the evidentiary standard of Sass Manufacturing (which Highland Foundry did not address)—and to build an evidentiary record capable of withstanding cross-examination and of showing that experimental castings are prototypes in the ordinary sense of a trial model, as discussed at paragraphs [18] to [20] of Highland Foundry—Pacific Alloy replaces generic shop travelers during the experimental phase with a Contemporaneous Experimental Heat Dossier (CEHD). First, a Pre-Heat Hypothesis Log is mandated under which no experimental heat under SRED-2026-04 may be poured without a signed, time-stamped single-page hypothesis sheet recording the specific independent variable being modified (for example, introducing a 0.08 wt% cerium-lanthanum rare-earth micro-alloying addition combined with embedded silicon-carbide chill blocks to accelerate interdendritic cooling through the 950°C to 650°C sensitizing window) alongside the quantitative predicted microstructural response. Second, during experimental pours, thermocouples embedded in the mould cavity at 25 mm, 75 mm, and 150 mm depths log real-time cooling curves (ΔT/Δt) directly to a time-stamped digital repository. Third, following each experimental heat, the metallurgist compiles a Post-Heat Analytical Synthesis containing scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental partitioning ratios between ferrite and austenite, and quantitative failure analyses explaining why the hypothesis succeeded or failed to suppress sigma-phase precipitation.
Step 3: Commercial Contract Terms and Risk Allocation Restructuring

To prevent ValveCo's $480,000 payment from being classified as a "contract payment" for SR&ED performed on ValveCo's behalf under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, legal counsel revises the commercial contract prior to execution. The contract is explicitly structured as a fixed-price commercial supply-of-goods agreement for 12 finished physical castings meeting performance specifications, rather than a contract for engineering or R&D services, and all references to prototype development fees or engineering reimbursement are excised from the purchase order and invoices. Furthermore, an explicit intellectual property retention clause is inserted stipulating that all background and foreground metallurgical processes, alloy modification chemistries, gating and risering methodologies, solidification models, and experimental test data developed by Pacific Alloy remain the sole and exclusive intellectual property and trade secrets of Pacific Alloy, while ValveCo acquires title solely to the twelve physical valve body castings meeting the mechanical acceptance criteria upon delivery. The contract also stipulates that payment is strictly contingent upon delivery of conforming commercial units, placing 100% of the financial and technical risk of failed experimental heats on Pacific Alloy. Under the CRA's Contract Payment Policy and Tax Court jurisprudence, retaining intellectual property ownership and bearing full financial risk of technical failure establishes that the SR&ED is undertaken by Pacific Alloy on its own behalf, preserving 100% of the expenditure base from contract-payment reductions.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Financial Cost Segregation Systems

To satisfy subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) expenditure verification requirements, Pacific Alloy implements discrete work-order time tracking and material segregation. Shop-floor personnel—including metallurgists, patternmakers, moulders, furnace operators, and lab technicians—badge into work order SRED-2026-04 via biometric shop terminals only when preparing, pouring, heat-treating, or destructively testing experimental trial castings, whereas hours spent pouring the 12 commercial castings under PROD-8841 are logged strictly to the commercial ledger. Simultaneously, raw alloys, chromite sand, and sacrificial thermocouples used in failed experimental heats that are scrapped or destructively sectioned are tracked under an SR&ED Materials Consumed general ledger sub-account, adjusted for any scrap remelt recovery value. Conversely, if an experimental prototype casting from the final validation heat passes non-destructive testing and is sold to ValveCo as one of the 12 commercial units, the material cost of that salable casting is transferred out of the SR&ED claim, ensuring full compliance with statutory expenditure rules.
Case Study 2: Industrial Heavy Equipment Manufacturer — Experimental Development of a Closed-Loop Thermal-Mechanical Die-Quenching System
Baseline Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Northern Mining Components Ltd. ("Northern Mining"), an Ontario-based manufacturer of heavy wear-resistant steel components and forging dies for the mining and forestry sectors, undertakes a project to develop an automated, closed-loop die-quenching and induction-tempering cell on its main shop floor. The technical objective is to manufacture ultra-high-strength, abrasion-resistant excavator bucket teeth (target core hardness of 58 HRC with high fracture toughness) using a novel low-alloy boron-manganese steel composition without the micro-cracking that occurs during conventional oil or polymer quenching.

In its unguided execution, Northern Mining commits four major legal and evidentiary errors of the kind commonly identified in SR&ED jurisprudence, most of which were not at issue in the Highland Foundry decision. First, regarding the "prototype machine" over-claim, Northern Mining constructs the entire $1.8 million automated manufacturing cell—including standard commercial CNC robotic arms, standard structural steel safety cages, commercial hydraulic presses, and off-the-shelf conveyors—and claims the entire $1.8 million capital and material cost as an experimental prototype system, even though most of the cell consists of standard commercial equipment that was not itself the subject of experimental development (Highland Foundry Ltd. holds only that a genuine prototype's continued commercial use does not by itself disqualify its cost) and capital expenditures made after 2013 are no longer eligible SR&ED expenditures. Second, engineers spend 4,000 hours programming standard programmable logic controller (PLC) user interfaces, factory ERP database integrations, and safety interlocks alongside 1,200 hours developing a real-time acoustic-emission and infrared pyrometry feedback algorithm to modulate high-pressure mist-quench nozzles during martensitic phase transformation, lumping all 5,200 hours into a single cost center (ENG-CELL-01). Third, during a three-month commissioning and trial run phase, the plant processes 15,000 bucket teeth through the cell, selling 11,500 of them to mining customers while claiming 100% of the plant's shop-floor wages and steel billet costs for those three months as SR&ED. Fourth, during the subsequent CRA audit, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) classifies the entire project as commercial plant commissioning and routine automation integration, disallowing the claim in full.
Step 1: Project Governance and Subsystem Isolation Architecture

To survive judicial scrutiny under the Highland Foundry decision—and to apply paragraphs [18] to [20], under which a trial model remains a prototype in the ordinary sense even if it continues in use after the experimental phase—Northern Mining must decompose the macro-capital project into eligible experimental sub-projects versus excluded commercial capital infrastructure at project inception. The Vice President of Engineering establishes an SR&ED Steering Committee that separates the $1.8 million capital build into two distinct accounting and technical buckets. Standard CNC robotics, material handling conveyors, hydraulic framing, PLC safety interlocks, and ERP integration are assigned to CAP-CELL-100, capitalized as standard depreciable property under Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) Class 53 or Class 8, and excluded entirely from the SR&ED claim.

Concurrently, the core SR&ED experimental sub-project (SRED-QUENCH-200) is restricted strictly to resolving the technological uncertainty of controlling non-linear heat-flux extraction rates (q″ > 12 MW/m2) across complex three-dimensional forging geometries during the martensite start (Ms) to martensite finish (Mf) phase transition (320°C to 140°C) to prevent transformation-induced residual tensile stress cracking. Rather than claiming the entire commercial production cell as a prototype, Northern Mining constructs a dedicated, modular Experimental Quench Test Rig—consisting of custom atomizing nozzle arrays, high-frequency acoustic emission sensors, and multi-wavelength thermal imaging arrays—mounted temporarily inside the cell. This isolation is consistent with the ordinary dictionary meaning of a prototype (a trial model or preliminary version) applied in paragraphs [18] to [20] of Highland Foundry Ltd.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Evidence Protocols

To prevent the CRA or the Tax Court from characterizing the work as routine plant commissioning or trial production, the engineering team establishes a formal fractional-factorial Design of Experiments (DoE) matrix prior to running shop-floor trials. Each test series is assigned a specific hypothesis code, such as evaluating whether pulsed atomized water-air mist modulation at 45 Hz synchronized with real-time surface pyrometry can equalize the Biot number (Bi) across variable 15 mm to 85 mm tooth cross-sections, thereby reducing residual surface tensile stress below 250 MPa. For the control algorithm development, software engineers maintain a dedicated Git repository exclusively for the thermodynamic predictive control model, where every code commit message references the specific physical experiment identifier (DoE-4.1 through DoE-4.8) and records why previous control equations failed to compensate for the Leidenfrost vapour-blanket collapse on the steel surface. Rather than relying on commercial hardness spot-checks, the team archives X-ray diffraction (XRD) residual stress maps, retained austenite volume fraction measurements, and acoustic emission crack-detection spectrograms for each experimental run.
Step 3: Commercial Contract Terms and Supplier or Customer Arrangements

Northern Mining retains an external automation integrator to build the standard robotic cell (CAP-CELL-100) and a specialized Canadian university metallurgical laboratory to perform XRD residual stress analysis (SRED-QUENCH-200), structuring these engagements under two separate legal agreements. The university laboratory contract contains an explicit SR&ED Subcontractor Statement of Work detailing the exact analytical tests performed directly in support of SRED-QUENCH-200 within Canada, ensuring that the payments qualify as eligible third-party subcontractor SR&ED expenditures at the statutory 80% inclusion rate under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Furthermore, during the experimental development window, Northern Mining contractually and operationally prohibits the fulfillment of commercial customer orders from scheduled DoE runs. Any bucket teeth produced during experimental DoE runs that are not destructively sectioned are quarantined in a segregated inventory lot (LOT-EXP-HOLD) so that commercial sales revenue and production costs are never commingled with experimental trial runs.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Financial Cost Segregation Systems

To establish unassailable expenditure eligibility under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, Northern Mining institutes granular activity-based time tracking across three mandatory task codes. Engineers and shop technicians log hours to TASK-SRED-CORE when formulating thermodynamic hypotheses, designing experimental nozzle geometries, writing predictive phase-transformation algorithms, and executing controlled DoE test runs, which are claimed at 100%. Hours spent machining sacrificial test coupons, calibrating pyrometers for DoE runs, and performing XRD and metallographic analysis commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the DoE trials under subsection 248(1) are logged to TASK-SRED-SUPPORT and claimed at 100%. Conversely, hours spent installing commercial robotics, programming standard PLC user interfaces, erecting safety guarding, and running post-validation commercial production batches are logged to TASK-COMM-INSTALL and excluded at 0%. Finally, by enforcing a strict experimental run cut-off, instead of claiming 15,000 commercial units over a three-month commissioning period, Northern Mining claims only the exact 180 sacrificial steel forgings consumed during the 12 documented DoE experimental runs (totaling 64 hours of dedicated experimental machine time), completely insulating the claim from disallowance under the commercial production exclusion of Regulation 2900(1)(h).
Summary Table of Remedial Governance Controls

The following table synthesizes the operational and legal controls implemented across both remedial case studies to satisfy the statutory and evidentiary standards of SR&ED jurisprudence, including the prototype and timing principles of Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994).

headers: Remedial Protocol Under Highland Foundry Standard

cells: Project Charter & Scope
Single commercial job number covering both R&D trials and commercial production runs.
Dual-track charter separating SRED experimental validation from PROD commercial fulfillment via a signed Technical Freeze Certificate.
Prevents automatic disqualification under the commercial production exclusion (ITR s. 2900(1)(h) / ITA s. 248(1)).
Prototype Characterization
Claiming entire multi-unit custom customer orders or full commercial manufacturing lines as "prototypes".
Restricting prototype claims to sacrificial test blocks, first-article validation castings, and modular experimental test rigs evaluated under the ordinary meaning of a prototype as a trial model.

Aligns directly with paragraphs [18]–[20] of Highland Foundry Ltd. regarding the ordinary (dictionary) meaning of prototypes, under which continued commercial use does not by itself disqualify a genuine prototype.
Experimental Methodology
Simultaneous, undocumented shop-floor adjustments to get a commercial part past QA inspection.
Formal Pre-Heat Hypothesis Logs and Design of Experiments (DoE) matrices isolating independent variables with quantitative lab analysis.
Satisfies the Sass Manufacturing and Regulation 2900(1) requirement for a "systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis".
Contractual Architecture
Accepting customer POs that reimburse "prototype engineering" or transfer process IP to the buyer.
Supply-of-goods contracts where the manufacturer retains 100% of process IP/trade secrets and bears full financial risk of failed trials.
Eliminates the "contract payment" reduction under ITA s. 127(18) and proves SR&ED was performed on the taxpayer's own behalf.
Cost Accounting & Labour
Year-end percentage estimates of shop wages, utilities, and commingled raw material costs.
Biometric task-code time tracking (SRED-CORE, SRED-SUPPORT, COMM) and separate GL sub-accounts for scrapped vs. salable materials.
Discharges the taxpayer's burden of proof on expenditure eligibility under ITA s. 37(1) and s. 127(9).

body.text: Conclusion and Strategic Takeaways for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Highland Foundry Ltd. (August 1994) remains a vital touchstone in Canadian SR&ED tax jurisprudence. For corporate taxpayers operating in heavy industry, metallurgy, and custom manufacturing, the ruling demonstrates that the capital cost of a genuine prototype built in the course of SR&ED is not disqualified merely because the prototype succeeds and continues in commercial use, since the "all or substantially all" test is applied at the time the expenditure is incurred rather than over the asset's useful life (although capital expenditures made after 2013 are no longer eligible SR&ED expenditures). Equally important, for tax litigators and technical advisors challenging arbitrary audit denials at the Notice of Objection or Tax Court stage, Highland Foundry Ltd. provides decisive judicial authority: Interpretation Bulletins and Information Circulars are not law (paragraph [11]), statutory terms such as "prototype" carry their ordinary and grammatical meaning (paragraphs [18] to [20]), and reasonable ambiguity in the statute must be resolved in favour of the taxpayer (paragraph [33]).
